questions.explanation: Drugs that most commonly cause obsessive-compulsive and related disorder include amphetamines and related substances, cocaine, and some heavy metals and toxins (e.g., carbon monoxide).

questions.question_text: The secondary use model for dual diagnosis proposes that patients use substances primarily for which reason?

options.text: To self-medicate symptoms and reduce dysphoria and social isolation

correct_answer.text: To self-medicate symptoms and reduce dysphoria and social isolation

questions.explanation: The secondary use model proposes that patients use substances in the first place to alleviate dysphoria or to self-medicate symptoms and reduce social isolation. This is the self-medication hypothesis, distinct from the common factor and supersensitivity models.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which treatments encourages participation in organized groups that help achieve and maintain recovery from alcohol use disorder?
questions.explanation: Twelvestep facilitation (TSF) is an empirically supported therapy that, as its name suggests, facilitates attendance 86 • PSYCHIATRY at recovery groups, including Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, Gamblers Anonymous, and so forth. TSF involves educating the patient about the content, format, and structure of mutual help groups early during treatment and then continuing to monitor the patient’s reactions and responses to meeting attendance. Interventions that incorporate TSF have been shown to enhance patients’ outcomes by approximately 10% to 20% over, outcomes achieved with standard CBT. AlAnon is a support group for close family and friends of those with alcohol use disorder.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old woman with cocaine dependence (first use at 18 years, current daily use) presents after 3 years of use. Her consumption pattern is notably different from typical cocaine users. Which factor best explains this deviation?

options.text: She initiated use early (earlier initiation predicts longer use)
She is using daily (frequency/intensity accelerates progression)
She is of White ethnicity (higher hazardous drinking rates in White populations)
She is in the age range where use typically begins

correct_answer.text: She is using daily (frequency/intensity accelerates progression)

questions.explanation: That average powder cocaine duration is 4.4 years among regular users. This patient at 3 years is approaching that average despite only 3 years elapsed since age 18 initiation (which is typical). Daily use intensity accelerates the trajectory and dependency development compared to occasional use patterns. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which laboratory tests is the best measure of recent heavy alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: Both GGT and CDT are laboratory indicators of heavy alcohol consumption, but CDT has higher sensitivity and specificity than GGT. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., p. 495). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: In DSM-IV, caffeine withdrawal was included in Appendix B as a criteria set provided for further study. which of the following options statements correctly describes how caffeine withdrawal is classified in DSM-5?

options.text: Caffeine withdrawal is no longer considered a valid psychiatric diagnosis.
Caffeine withdrawal remains a proposed diagnosis in DSM-5 and is included in “Conditions for Further Study” in Section III.
Caffeine withdrawal is classified under other (or unknown) substance withdrawal in DSM-5.
Caffeine withdrawal is classified under stimulant withdrawal in DSM-5.
Caffeine withdrawal was moved to the main body of DSM-5 and is now included in the “Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders” chapter.

correct_answer.text: Caffeine withdrawal was moved to the main body of DSM-5 and is now included in the “Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders” chapter.

questions.explanation: Caffeine withdrawal was moved from Appendix B, “Criteria Sets and Axes Provided for Further Study,” in DSM-IV to the main body of DSM-5; it is now included among the Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders. While caffeine withdrawal can mimic other drug withdrawal states (e.g., from amphetamines, cocaine), caffeine withdrawal is considered distinct from stimulant withdrawal.

questions.question_text: Best evidence base to decrease alcohol harm is

options.text: Education of public about harm of alcohol

questions.explanation: When other factors are held constant, such as income and the price of other goods, a rise in alcohol prices leads to less alcohol consumption and vice versa. Price increases reduce the harms caused by alcohol and can also indicate that heavier drinking has been reduced. Policies that increase alcohol prices delay the initiation of drinking, slow young people's progression towards drinking larger amounts and reduce heavy drinking among them. Setting a minimum price per gram of alcohol can be as effective as an across- theboard increase in tax, with both options costing heavy consumers far in excess of the cost to light consumers. Natural experiments in Europe consequent to economic treaties have shown that as alcohol taxes and prices have gone down, so sales and alcohol consumption have usually increased. (From Evidence for the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of interventions to reduce alcohol-related harm, WHO 2009).

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found unresponsive in a public toilet. On examination, he has pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate of 6 breaths/minute, reduced consciousness (GCS 8/15), and bradycardia (heart rate 48 bpm). Track marks are visible on his forearms. Which substance has he most likely used?
questions.explanation: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness—classic opioid toxicity presentation.

questions.question_text: A 62-year-old with chronic alcohol dependence undergoing detoxification has no clinical or radiological signs of Wernicke\'s encephalopathy and no other complications. According to the source evidence base, what is the minimum daily dose of thiamine for prophylaxis?

options.text: 250 mg parenterally once daily for 3–5 days
500 mg parenterally once daily for 3–5 days

questions.explanation:
According to The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry (15th Edition, 2025), the recommended minimum daily prophylactic dose of thiamine during alcohol detoxification depends on the route of administration:

Oral Thiamine Prophylaxis: The recommended dose is 300 mg daily orally during assisted alcohol withdrawal and periods of continued alcohol intake for individuals without neuropsychiatric complications
- Parenteral Thiamine Prophylaxis: In patients at higher risk or undergoing inpatient/community-assisted detoxification without overt signs of Wernicke\'s encephalopathy, the prophylactic dose is 200 mg to 300 mg once daily given intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) for 3 to 5 days

questions.question_text: Pathological intoxication is characterized by severe behavioural reaction developing rapidly after consumption of a small amount of alcohol. Which of the following is NOT a proposed predisposing factor?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists advancing age, brain damage, high levels of underlying anxiety, using sedative-hypnotic drugs, and feeling fatigued as proposed predisposing factors for pathological intoxication. Chronic heavy drinking pattern is not mentioned as a predisposing factor. Evidence emphasizes that the reaction occurs after consumption of a *small* amount of alcohol, which contrasts with chronic heavy drinking. ---

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman with a 10-year history of daily cannabis use reports spending most of her free time obtaining, using, and recovering from cannabis. She has stopped attending social activities and hobbies she previously enjoyed. Which Edwards & Gross criterion best describes her presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient demonstrates narrowed repertoire—the restriction of her behavioural patterns to cannabis-related activities, with abandonment of previously valued leisure activities. This is the first Edwards & Gross criterion. Subjective awareness of compulsion might also apply, but narrowed repertoire more directly describes her restricted behavioural repertoire.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is classified as a Class B drug under the 1971 Misuse of Drugs Act?
questions.explanation: Methylphenidate (Ritalin) is explicitly listed as a Class B drug. Cannabis, GHB, and ketamine are Class C; cocaine is Class A. This distinction reflects the legal risk profile assigned to each substance. ---

questions.question_text: The mortality rate in a person being treated for alcohol withdrawal delirium is
questions.explanation: Alcohol dependence occurs in 15–20% of hospitalized patients in some settings. Hence withdrawal from alcohol is also a common presentation in this population. Withdrawal symptoms are minor in most cases, but they can be considerable and even fatal in some. Alcohol withdrawal delirium, commonly known as delirium tremens or ‘DTs’, is the most serious manifestation of alcohol withdrawal syndrome. Classic studies quote a mortality of around 15%, but with advances in treatment, mortality rates have fallen, and more recent studies indicate a mortality of 0 to 1% in treated cases. Mayo-Smith MF, Beecher LH, Fischer TL, et al. Management of alcohol withdrawal delirium: an evidence-based practice guideline. Archives of Internal Medicine 2004; 164: 1405–1412.

questions.question_text: Which drug is classified as Class C under the 1971 Misuse of Drugs Act?
questions.explanation: The source lists ketamine as a Class C drug. Heroin, crack cocaine, LSD, and methylamphetamine are all Class A drugs, making ketamine the only correct Class C option among these choices. ---

questions.question_text: In most substance/medication-induced mental disorders (with the exception of substance/medication-induced major or mild neurocognitive disorder and hallucinogen persisting perception disorder), if the person abstains from substance use, the disorder will eventually disappear or no longer be clinically relevant even without formal treatment. In what time frame is this likely to happen?

options.text: “Relatively quickly” but no specific period of time.

questions.explanation: Although the symptoms of substance/medication-induced mental disorders can be identical to those of independent mental disorders (e.g., delusions, hallucinations, psychoses, major depressive episodes, anxiety syndromes), and although they can have the same severe consequences (e.g., suicide), most induced mental disorders are likely to improve relatively quickly with abstinence and are unlikely to remain clinically relevant for more than 1 month after complete cessation of use.

questions.question_text: Pathological intoxication is characterised by rapid severe behavioural reaction after consumption of what quantity of alcohol?
questions.explanation: Pathological intoxication as a severe behavioural reaction developing rapidly after consumption of a small amount of alcohol. This distinguishes it from typical intoxication patterns and is the defining characteristic of this idiosyncratic reaction.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which substance use disorders is more common among adolescent males than among adolescent females?

options.text: A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder.
A diagnosis of phencyclidine (PCP) use disorder.
Sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder.
Stimulant use disorder, amphetamine-type substance subtype.

questions.explanation: Although for the majority of substances the prevalence of a substance use disorder is higher in adult men versus women, among adolescents there are a number of substances in which this trend is reversed. The 12-month prevalence of stimulant use disorder, cocaine subtype among 12- to 17-year-olds is greater in males (0.4%) relative to females (0.1%). The 12-month prevalence of other hallucinogen use disorder is slightly higher in adolescent females (0.6%) than in males (0.4%). For 12- to 17-year-olds, the rate of sedative, hypnotic, or Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 401 anxiolytic use disorder in females (0.4%) exceeds that of males (0.2%). Among 12to 17-year-olds, the rate of stimulant use disorder, amphetamine-type substance subtype in females (0.3%) is greater than the rate in males (0.1%). The rate of inhalant use disorder is 0.4% in both 12- to 17-year-old boys and girls. Of note, adolescent males are overall more likely than adolescent females to experiment with and use substances.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man presents with a 6-year history of daily cannabis use, multiple failed attempts to reduce consumption, and has organized his life around obtaining and using cannabis. Which Edwards & Gross criterion is MOST prominently demonstrated?
questions.explanation: The vignette describes organizing life around drug use and failed reduction attempts, which exemplifies narrowed repertoire – the reduction of varied activities and social engagement due to centralization around the substance. While salience is also present, the description of life organization specifically illustrates repertoire narrowing. This requires linking clinical presentation to specific dependence criteria. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which illicit substance use disorders is most prevalent in the United States?

options.text: A diagnosis of cocaine use disorder
A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder
A diagnosis of phencyclidine use disorder
A diagnosis of stimulant use disorder
A diagnosis of opioid use disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder

questions.explanation: Cannabinoids, especially cannabis, are the most commonly used illicit psychoactive substances in the United States.

questions.question_text: A individual with opioid dependence (DSM-I V-T R)/ opioid use disorder (DSM5) comes to the emergency room seeking opiate detox. He states that his last use was just a couple of hours ago. Physical exam and labs, including a standard urine toxicology, are negative. Which of the following was the individual most likely taking?
questions.explanation: Many standard urine tests detect only naturally occurring opiates that are derived from the opium poppy. Semisynthetic or synthetic opioids such as oxycodone, hydromorphone, hydrocodone, methadone, fentanyl, and buprenorphine are often not detected by standard urine drug testing and require more specific tests. Several “expanded opioid panels” exist, but specific testing varies by site.

questions.question_text: The acronym ‘FRAMES’ in brief clinical measure for alcohol dependence stands for all with the exception of
questions.explanation: The acronym FRAMES captures the essence of a number of interventions commonly used under the terms ‘brief intervention’. These are interventions that cover a range from one 5-minute interaction to several 45-minute sessions. The major positive studies discussed in this section typically consist of one interaction lasting between 5 and 20 minutes, sometimes with one brief follow-up contact. The acronym FRAMES stands for: feedback: about personal risk or impairment; responsibility: emphasis on personal responsibility for change; advice: to cut down or abstain if indicated because of severe dependence or harm; menu: of alternative options for changing drinking pattern and, jointly with the patient, setting a target; intermediate goals of reduction can be a start; empathic interviewing: listening refl ectively without cajoling or confronting; exploring with patients the reasons for change as they see their situation; self-effi cacy: an interviewing style that enhances people’s belief in their ability to change. ‘Rolling with resistance’ is a part of Miller and Rollnick’s motivational interviewing. SIGN guidelines No: 74; The management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence in primary care. http://www.sign.ac.uk/guidelines/fulltext/74/index.html

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients who undergo untreated sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic withdrawal experience a grand mal seizure?
questions.explanation: A grand mal seizure may occur in as many as 20%–30% of individuals undergoing untreated withdrawal from sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic substances.

questions.question_text: Tolerance doesn’t develop to which of the following symptoms/signs in opiate dependence?
questions.explanation: Recent research has shed new light on the mechanisms involved in the development of opioid tolerance and dependence. Stimulation of opioid receptors located on critical cells such as those located in the locus coeruleus produces a decrease in cell fi ring. This effect refl ects cellular hyperpolarization that results from both the activation of potassium channels and the inhibition of slowly depolarizing sodium channels. These actions occur in conjunction with a decrease in intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. Among the given choices, both constipation and miosis have been traditionally thought to be resistant to tolerance. Kollars and Larson reviewed the two studies conducted in the late 60s which are often quoted to show that miosis does not develop tolerance. They quote a number of other studies which have shown that miosis is susceptible to tolerance. There are comparatively few data refuting the lack of tolerance response for constipation. Clinical experience hints that constipation is a major problem that persists without development of tolerance, especially in elderly people who are prescribed opiates as analgesics. This can be very diffi cult to treat, at times requiring enemas and in severe cases requiring manual evacuation. Kollars JP and Larson M. tolerance to miotic effects of opioids. Anesthesiology: 2005; 102: 701. Higgins S, Stitzer M, McCaul M, et al. Pupillary response to methadone challenge in heroin users. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics 1985; 37: 460–463.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic with clear sensorium presents with auditory hallucinations that began 5 days ago, shortly after his last drink, and are improving. Over the next 3 months without relapse, the hallucinations completely resolve. What clinical course information most supports the diagnosis of alcoholic hallucinosis?

options.text: The atypical onset during early withdrawal rather than intoxication
The clear sensorium, onset after alcohol use, improvement during abstinence, and resolution timeframe of less than 6 months

correct_answer.text: The clear sensorium, onset after alcohol use, improvement during abstinence, and resolution timeframe of less than 6 months

questions.explanation: Multiple features support alcoholic hallucinosis diagnosis: (1) clear sensorium distinguishes it from delirium tremens, (2) onset temporally related to alcohol cessation, (3) improvement and resolution during abstinence (a key distinguishing feature from schizophrenia), and (4) resolution within 6 months (Evidence notess hallucinations persisting >6 months should raise suspicion of schizophrenia). The constellation of these clinical features makes alcoholic hallucinosis most likely.

questions.question_text: Which observation supports the common factor model over the secondary use model in dual diagnosis?

options.text: Patients with dual diagnosis have more relatives with substance use disorder, while relatives of substance-free SMI patients do not show increased SUD
All severe mental illness develops before substance use
Substance use always precedes mental illness onset
Mental illness and SUD respond to the same medications
Environmental stress is the sole determinant of both conditions

correct_answer.text: Patients with dual diagnosis have more relatives with substance use disorder, while relatives of substance-free SMI patients do not show increased SUD

questions.explanation: That patients with dual diagnosis have more relatives with substance use disorder, but relatives of substance-free but severely mentally ill patients do not have an increase in substance use disorder. This pattern of familial aggregation supports shared genetic or constitutional factors (common factor model) rather than one condition directly causing the other (secondary use or secondary illness models). The genetic loading suggests shared vulnerability.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old with 3 years of ecstasy use reports using the drug approximately monthly at social gatherings, experiencing no withdrawal symptoms, and maintaining stable employment and relationships. According to epidemiological patterns in the source, how does this patient's drug trajectory compare to average ecstasy users?

options.text: Unusually high frequency compared to peers

questions.explanation: Average duration of ecstasy use among regular users is 3.9 years. A 3-year user at monthly frequency is within the expected range. This requires understanding epidemiological duration data and comparing individual patterns to population norms, linking two concepts. ---

questions.question_text: According to the source, the term dependence is best understood as:

options.text: A moral failing of the individual
A medical concept independent of moral judgement
A reversible state requiring no treatment

correct_answer.text: A medical concept independent of moral judgement

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Dependence is not a moral, but a medical concept. This emphasizes the biomedical model and removes stigmatizing language. The concept applies to various substances and has treatment implications.

questions.question_text: A chronic alcoholic patient presents with memory gaps lasting several hours, during which he drove home and performed complex driving maneuvers, yet remembers none of these activities the next day. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: Alcohol-related blackouts as discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. The patient demonstrates performing complex tasks without later recall, with memory disruption during intoxication—the defining feature of blackouts. Korsakoff's syndrome is a chronic syndrome; confabulation is memory falsification.

questions.question_text: In the context of dual diagnosis between SMI and SUD, which clinical observation would most directly contradict the common factor model?

options.text: Dual diagnosis patients have relatives with SUD
SMI-free patients with SUD have relatives with SMI
SMI-free substance-abusers have no increase in family SMI rates
Substance-free SMI patients have no increase in family SUD rates
The temporal sequence of illness onset is unpredictable

correct_answer.text: Substance-free SMI patients have no increase in family SUD rates

questions.explanation: This is a 2-step logical reasoning question. The common factor model proposes a shared genetic vulnerability predisposing to both conditions. Evidence shows that relatives of dual diagnosis patients have increased SUD rates (supporting the model), but relatives of substance-free but severely mentally ill patients (SMI) do not have an increase in substance use disorder. This finding actually supports the model by showing specificity. However, if substance-free SMI patients had NO increase in family SUD (option D), this would be the most direct evidence against the model, as it would suggest no shared genetic loading. ---

questions.question_text: In chronic alcoholics, approximately what percentage exhibit signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: In some case series, nearly one-eighths, i.e. 12.5% of all chronic alcoholics exhibited signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy. This highlights the significant burden of this complication in the chronic alcoholic population.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach uses conditioned responses and controlled exposure to substance-related cues in alcohol rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy uses controlled presentation of alcohol or substance cues to establish conditioned responses and reduce craving through repeated exposure in the absence of reinforcement, operating through principles of behavioral conditioning.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the most widely abused recreational substance among high school students in the United States?
questions.explanation: Cannabis is the most widely used recreational substance among high school students in the United States. About 35% of 12th graders have reported using cannabis, compared with about 15% for alcohol. The other options have variable rates of abuse among high school students but do not surpass cannabis use.

questions.question_text: According to the source's description of Magnus Huss's concept of alcoholism (1865), which of the following did he NOT include?
questions.explanation: That Huss's 1865 concept of alcoholism included dependence, acute alcohol-related health issues and cumulative social problems. Genetic predisposition is not mentioned as part of his historical definition.

questions.question_text: A man doesn't think drinking alcohol is a problem and doesn't want to quit. According to Prochaska's model, which stage is he in?
questions.explanation: In pre-contemplation stage, the user does not recognize that problem use exists, although this may be increasingly obvious to those around them

questions.question_text: How long can a urine drug screen test stay positive for delta9- tetrahydrocannabinol in a heavy cannabis user?
questions.explanation: In frequent, heavy cannabis users THC is stored in adipose tissue and its metabolite 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC (THCCOOH) is excreted slowly, so urine screens can remain positive for several weeks — typically 2–4 weeks after last use (DSM-5-TR, p.798: \'In frequent users, urine tests for THCCOOH often remain positive for weeks after last use\'). Shorter windows (12–24 hours, 4–6 days, 1–2 weeks) apply to single or occasional/moderate use rather than chronic heavy use. Option B is not a duration and is not a valid answer.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old develops hallucinations and confusion within 30 minutes of consuming one alcoholic drink at a social gathering. He becomes psychomotor agitated, aggressive, and disoriented. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical features match pathological intoxication: severe behavioural reaction (confusion, hallucinations, psychomotor agitation, aggression) developing rapidly after a small amount of alcohol. Delirium tremens is a withdrawal syndrome; alcoholic hallucinosis develops in chronic alcoholics with clear sensorium; this acute dyscontrol after minimal alcohol is characteristic of idiosyncratic intoxication.

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old male with 15 years of alcohol dependence presents with concerns about his drinking pattern. The source indicates that patients like him have an approximate age at death of:
questions.explanation: The age at death is around 60 years – very premature for alcohol dependent patients. This represents a significant reduction in life expectancy compared to the general population.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old woman reports that she has lost interest in her previous hobbies (painting, yoga, socialising with non-drinking friends) since increasing her cocaine use. Most of her time is now spent obtaining and using cocaine. This pattern best demonstrates which concept?
questions.explanation: Narrowed repertoire describes the restriction of activities and interests exclusively to substance-related behaviours, with abandonment of alternative activities and pleasures. This patient demonstrates exactly this pattern—loss of previous activities with complete focus on cocaine use.

questions.question_text: A decrease in which of the following subtypes of dopamine receptors makes an individual susceptible to relapse in a population with substance use?
questions.explanation: Decreased D2 receptors in alcohol, cocaine, and methamphetamine users, whether premorbid or the consequence of substance use, in conjunction with a fi nding of increased salience to drug cues, indicate susceptibility to relapse in this population. Chang L and Haning W. Insights from recent positron emission tomographic studies of drug abuse and dependence. Current Opinions in Psychiatry 19: 246–252.

questions.question_text: In the United Kingdom, one unit of alcohol is equivalent to which of the following?
questions.explanation: In the United Kingdom, a unit is 8 grams of pure alcohol, equivalent to half a pint of ordinary beer, a small glass of wine (9% strength), or one measure of spirits. In the USA a single drink is usually considered to contain about 12 grams of ethanol, which is the content of 12 ounces of beer, one 4-ounce glass of non-fortifi ed wine, or 1–1.5 ounces of 40% ethanol liquor (e.g. whiskey or gin). Using moderate sizes of drinks, clinicians estimate that a single ‘drink’ (1.5 units) increases the blood alcohol level of a 150-pound man by 15–20 mg/dL, which is about the concentration of alcohol that an average person can metabolize in 1 hour. Murray RM, Kendler KS, McGuffi n P, et al. Essential Psychiatry, 4th edn. Cambridge University Press, 2008, p. 199.

questions.question_text: Magnus Huss coined the term 'alcoholism' in which year?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Magnus Huss in 1865 coined 'alcoholism.' This is straightforward factual recall from the historical section. ---

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old reports first cannabis use at 14 years and now uses 4–5 times weekly. He has used continuously for 2 years. How does this duration compare to the population average for regular cannabis users?
questions.explanation: That among regular users, average cannabis duration is 6.2 years. This patient's 2-year duration is substantially shorter, though his frequency (4–5 times weekly) suggests high engagement despite limited duration. ---

questions.question_text: Neuroadaptation differs from dependence primarily in which aspect?
questions.explanation: Neuroadaptation as a state where discontinuation, loss of effect, and relief from discontinuation can occur (as with SSRIs), but crucially, no active drug-seeking behaviour develops. This distinguishes it from true dependence. ---

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with 30 years of alcohol dependence, complicated by cirrhosis and cognitive impairment. He asks if the age of first intoxication in alcohol-dependent patients differs from the general population. What does the source suggest?

options.text: Dependent drinkers have significantly earlier first intoxication
Dependent drinkers have significantly later first intoxication
Age at first intoxication is essentially the same as the general population
Age at first intoxication cannot be determined from available data
Dependent drinkers have more variable ages of first intoxication

correct_answer.text: Age at first intoxication is essentially the same as the general population

questions.question_text: What is the hallmark feature of caffeine withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Headache is the hallmark feature of caffeine withdrawal. The remaining options are also symptoms of caffeine withdrawal and could occur in absence of headache. Caffeine is the most widely consumed behaviorally active drug in the world. Because caffeine ingestion is often integrated into social customs and daily rituals (e.g., coffee break, tea time), some caffeine consumers may be unaware of their physical dependence on caffeine and thus withdrawal symptoms could be unexpected and misattributed to other causes (e.g., the flu, migraine). Caffeine withdrawal symptoms may occur when individuals are required to abstain from foods and beverages prior to medical procedures or when a usual caffeine dose is missed because of a change in routine (e.g., during travel, weekends).

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which laboratory tests can be used in combination with gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) to monitor abstinence from alcohol?

options.text: A diagnosis of mean corpuscular volume (MCV).

questions.explanation: Elevation of GGT is a sensitive laboratory indicator of heavy drinking. At least 70% of individuals with a high GGT level are persistent heavy drinkers (i.e., consuming eight or more drinks daily on a regular basis). A second test with comparable or even higher levels of sensitivity and specificity is CDT, with levels of 20 units or higher useful in identifying individuals who regularly consume eight or more drinks daily. Since both GGT and CDT levels return toward normal within days to weeks of stopping drinking, both state markers are useful in monitoring abstinence, especially when the clinician observes increases, rather than decreases, in these values over time. The combination of CDT and GGT may have even higher levels of sensitivity and specificity than either test used alone. Although the MCV can be used to help identify those who drink heavily, it is a poor method of monitoring abstinence because of the long half-life of red blood cells. Liver function tests (e.g., ALT and alkaline phosphatase) can reveal liver injury that is a consequence of heavy drinking. Nonspecific elevations of lipid levels in the blood (e.g., triglycerides and lipoprotein cholesterol) may also be observed due to decreases in gluconeogenesis associated with heavy drinking.
